templates.name: Main idea, informational study report (incl. explainer and scholar-argument passages)

items.passage: Bumble bees (Bombus impatiens) that consume sunflower pollen harbor far less intense infections of the gut parasite Crithidia bombi than do bees fed other pollen. Hypothesizing that sunflower pollen alters the composition of the microbial community in a bee’s gut, Rachel Yost, Alison Fowler, and Lynn Adler inoculated bees with gut material from donors raised on either sunflower or buckwheat pollen; all recipients subsequently received wildflower pollen and were then exposed to the parasite. Recipients of material from sunflower-fed donors became infected as frequently, and as intensely, as recipients of material from buckwheat-fed donors.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the protection that sunflower pollen gives bumble bees against Crithidia bombi?
options: It likely spreads through a colony as bees pass gut microbes to one another, since gut material was transferred from bee to bee in the study.
It likely arises from something other than the gut microbes found in bees that have eaten sunflower pollen.
It likely is shared by buckwheat pollen, since bees given gut material from buckwheat-fed donors were infected no more heavily than the others.
It likely becomes stronger when bees eat wildflower pollen in addition to sunflower pollen.
items.explanation: The researchers tested the idea that sunflower pollen protects bees by changing the microbes in their guts. But bees given gut material from sunflower-fed donors “became infected as frequently, and as intensely, as recipients of material from buckwheat-fed donors.” Since the microbes of sunflower-fed bees gave no protection, the protection likely comes from something else.

A.why_wrong: Gut material was transferred between bees, but the transfer gave the recipients no protection, so the study suggests that the protection does not pass from bee to bee this way.

C.recipe: twisted detail (equal result read as shared protection)
C.why_wrong: The two groups of recipients were infected equally because neither group was protected; the text indicates that bees fed pollen other than sunflower carry heavier infections, and the equal result says nothing in favor of buckwheat pollen.

D.why_wrong: Only the recipients, which never ate sunflower pollen, were fed wildflower pollen; the text never compares bees eating both kinds of pollen with bees eating sunflower pollen alone.

sources.what: Yost, Fowler, Adler 2023, Microbial Ecology: sunflower pollen dramatically reduces Crithidia bombi in Bombus impatiens; hypothesis that sunflower changes the gut microbiome; donors fed sunflower or buckwheat pollen, recipients inoculated with donor guts and fed wildflower pollen, then infected; no difference in infection presence or intensity; suggests the effect is not mediated by gut microbiota

items.notes: Natural science (entomology). Two-step chain: hypothesis that the protection works through gut microbes; transferred microbes from sunflower-fed bees gave no protection; so the protection must come from something else. The passage stops at the result and never states the conclusion (the abstract does). Author names (Rachel T. Yost, Alison E. Fowler, Lynn S. Adler) confirmed from the PubMed record. Band 6: each wrong option keeps a true detail (the transfer, the equal result, the wildflower diet) and fails on the link drawn from it.

review.note: Core claim matches the PubMed abstract (gut transplants from sunflower-fed donors gave no protection; effect not mediated by gut microbiota).

band7.why: Key needs two links (the stated hypothesis that the protection works through gut microbes, then the null transfer result) and never echoes the abstract's conclusion; A and C each start from a true detail (the transfer, the equal infection) and fail on the link drawn from it; D is the weakest option. CID hard cells are planned at band 6.

items.passage: Greek drinking vessels found at Vix-Mont Lassois and other Early Celtic princely sites of the 600s to 400s BCE, in present-day eastern France, Switzerland, and southwestern Germany, have long been interpreted as evidence that local elites were imitating the wine feasts of the Mediterranean world. Analyzing organic residues in 99 vessels from Vix, however, Maxime Rageot and colleagues determined that imported Greek wares and locally made pottery alike had contained not only grape wine but also other plant-based fermented beverages, and residues of millet and beehive products point to drinks prepared from local ingredients.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the Greek vessels used at Vix?
options: They likely held grape wine more often than the locally made pots did, since wine was the drink at the center of Mediterranean feasts.
They likely were made by local potters who copied Greek designs, since the local pots and the Greek wares held the same kinds of drinks.
They likely were prized mainly as displays of the elite’s trade connections and were seldom filled with drink.
They likely were used in keeping with local drinking customs rather than simply to reproduce Mediterranean feasts.
items.explanation: The vessels have “long been interpreted as evidence that local elites were imitating the wine feasts of the Mediterranean world.” Yet the residues show that the Greek wares, like local pottery, “had contained not only grape wine but also other plant-based fermented beverages,” and the residues “point to drinks prepared from local ingredients.” Because the imported vessels also held drinks other than wine, they were likely used according to local habits, not only to copy Mediterranean practice.

A.why_wrong: The text says that both kinds of vessel held grape wine; it never compares how often each held it.

B.recipe: twisted detail (imports turned into local copies)
B.why_wrong: The text calls the Greek wares “imported”; sharing the same drinks with local pots shows how they were used, not where they were made.

C.why_wrong: The residues found in the Greek vessels show that they were used to hold wine and other drinks, so they were not seldom filled.

sources.what: Rageot et al. 2019, PLoS ONE: imported vessels at Early Celtic princely sites (7th to 5th cent. BC, SW Germany, Switzerland, E France) long interpreted as elite imitation of Mediterranean wine feasting; residue analysis of 99 vessels from Vix-Mont Lassois; both Greek and local wares served grape wine and other plant-based fermented beverages; millet and beehive products important; appropriation of the foreign vessels

items.notes: Archaeology. Chain: the old view (imitation); both kinds of vessel held local fermented drinks; so the imports were adapted to local use (the paper's word is appropriation, which the passage does not use). Band 6: A and B start from a true detail (wine was imported in feasting culture; both held the same drinks) and draw the wrong conclusion; C is the plain contradiction.

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract (99 Vix vessels; Greek and local wares both held grape wine and other fermented drinks; appropriation).

band7.why: Key joins the old imitation reading with residues in both kinds of vessel and paraphrases the paper's appropriation as local custom; A and B keep true parts (wine as the feast drink, both wares holding the same drinks) but each fails on one stated word (alike, imported), so it sits at the lower edge of band 6.

items.passage:
The following text is from F. M. Mayor’s 1913 novel The Third Miss Symons. Henrietta, age nine, and her brother William are hiding together during a game. Amy is a friend Henrietta has imagined.

Henrietta never knew how it was that she told him about Amy. It had always been her firm resolve that this was to be her own dead secret, never revealed. But the unusual warmth of the interview went to her head. It was in a kind of intoxication of happiness that she poured out her confidence. The shrubbery was so dark that William’s face could not be seen, but he began fidgeting, and soon broke in: “I say, what hours the others are, it must be tea-time. Let’s go and find them.”
items.stem: Based on the text, how does William most likely react to what Henrietta tells him?
options: He is uneasy hearing her confidence and politely ends the conversation.
He is too worried about being late for tea to pay attention to what she is saying.
He is hurt that she has kept something so important from him until now.
He is so eager to tell the others her secret that he wants to find them at once.
items.explanation: While Henrietta “poured out her confidence,” William “began fidgeting, and soon broke in” with a remark about the others and tea. His restlessness and his sudden change of subject suggest that he feels awkward hearing her secret and gently ends the conversation.

B.why_wrong: William mentions tea, but he says it while interrupting her and fidgeting; the remark reads as a way to change the subject, and nothing suggests he had stopped listening out of worry about tea.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests William feels hurt; he responds by fidgeting and changing the subject, not by reproaching her.

D.why_wrong: William suggests finding the others, but the text gives no sign that he means to tell them her secret.

sources.what: F. M. Mayor, The Third Miss Symons (1913), chapter I, Project Gutenberg text (the hide-and-seek scene; the next sentence in the novel reads “It was kind of William to snub her confidence so gently”)

items.notes: Literary prose. Excerpt copied exactly, trimmed at sentence boundaries (the scene's opening sentences are replaced by the context line); Gutenberg's straight quotes and apostrophes made curly. The key is confirmed by the novel's next sentence (left out of the excerpt): “It was kind of William to snub her confidence so gently.” Model 3.2 (how characters regard someone, read from behavior). Band 6: B is the literal reading of the tea remark, C and D are motives the text never gives.

review.note: Excerpt checked word for word against Gutenberg 27071; the novel's next sentence (“It was kind of William to snub her confidence so gently”) confirms the key, including politely.

band7.why: Key reads the reaction from behavior (fidgeting, a tea-time pretext) rather than a stated feeling, and B is the literal reading of the tea remark that a hurried reader takes; C and D are motives the text never gives, so the item turns on one close distractor: lower band 6, not easier.

items.passage: Philosopher Kieran Setiya attributes a familiar form of midlife dissatisfaction to the structure of the activities people value. Telic activities, such as teaching a class or earning a raise, aim at a terminal state of completion, so that achieving them simultaneously exhausts one’s engagement with them; atelic activities, such as listening to music or spending time with friends, can be interrupted but never completed. A life organized predominantly around telic projects, Setiya argues, perpetually locates fulfillment in the future or the past; the remedy is not to relinquish such goals but to invest more fully in atelic pursuits.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Because telic activities end once achieved, Setiya recommends that people in midlife replace them with atelic ones.
According to Setiya, atelic activities grow more satisfying over time, whereas telic activities grow less so.
Setiya argues that midlife discontent may be eased by valuing pursuits that cannot be completed, without abandoning goals.
Setiya traces midlife discontent to people’s having completed so many projects that no new goals remain.
items.explanation: Setiya argues that a life organized “predominantly around telic projects” locates fulfillment “in the future or the past,” and that “the remedy is not to relinquish such goals but to invest more fully in atelic pursuits,” activities that “can be interrupted but never completed.” So the main idea is that midlife discontent may be eased by valuing atelic pursuits while keeping goal-directed ones.

A.why_wrong: Setiya says that the remedy “is not to relinquish such goals,” so he does not recommend replacing telic activities.

B.why_wrong: The text never says how satisfying either kind of activity becomes over time; it says only that atelic activities cannot be completed.

D.why_wrong: The text locates the problem in how telic activities work, keeping fulfillment in the future or the past; it never says that people run out of new goals.

sources.what: Kieran Setiya, Aeon essay drawn from Midlife: A Philosophical Guide (2017): telic activities aim at completion and exhaustion (teach a class, earn a raise); atelic activities (listening to music, spending time with friends) can be stopped but not completed; satisfaction always in the future or the past; solution is to invest more fully in atelic activities while not giving up worthwhile goals

items.notes: Humanities (philosophy). Scholar-argument passage like 3.20. The key must carry the concession (do not give up goals) and the hedge; A drops the concession, D gives a cause Setiya explicitly rejects in the source. Band 6.

review.note: Core claim matches Setiya's Aeon essay (telic vs atelic; do not give up worthwhile goals; invest more fully in atelic activities).

band7.why: Option A is ruled out by one quoted phrase (not to relinquish such goals), but it is the concession-dropping mirror a hurried reader picks, and the key must carry both the concession and the hedge (may be eased); B and D are an invented comparison and a cause Setiya rejects.

items.passage: The farming methods of the Green Revolution had relatively little impact in sub-Saharan Africa, and few of the technologies since proposed for the region’s rural areas have been rigorously evaluated. Jennifer Burney and colleagues assessed one such technology, solar-powered drip irrigation, in which pumps run by solar panels deliver water to the roots of crops. Comparing two villages in northern Benin where the systems were installed with two comparable villages lacking them, the researchers found that the systems significantly increased both household income and nutritional intake and were cost-effective compared with alternative technologies.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A study of villages in Benin suggests that solar-powered drip irrigation can raise rural households’ earnings and improve their diets at a competitive cost.
Burney and colleagues found that solar-powered drip irrigation raised household incomes in northern Benin more than any other farming technology that has been tested in sub-Saharan Africa.
Because few farming technologies have been rigorously evaluated in sub-Saharan Africa, the benefits that solar-powered drip irrigation offers rural households there remain largely uncertain.
Although solar-powered drip irrigation improved the diets of households in northern Benin, its cost relative to that of other technologies may make it impractical for most farmers.
items.explanation: The text notes that few technologies proposed for rural sub-Saharan Africa “have been rigorously evaluated” and then reports an evaluation of one: in northern Benin, solar-powered drip irrigation “significantly increased both household income and nutritional intake” and the systems “were cost-effective compared with alternative technologies.” So the main idea is that the study suggests this technology can improve rural households’ earnings and diets at a competitive cost.

B.why_wrong: The text says that the systems increased household income, but it compares only their cost-effectiveness with that of alternative technologies; it never says that they raised incomes more than any other technology.

C.recipe: contradicts the text (the setup read as the conclusion)
C.why_wrong: The text does say that few such technologies “have been rigorously evaluated,” but it then reports an evaluation that found clear benefits, so it does not present the benefits of this technology as uncertain.

D.recipe: contradicts the text (reverses the cost finding)
D.why_wrong: The researchers found that the systems “were cost-effective compared with alternative technologies,” so the text gives no reason to think that their cost makes them impractical.

sources.what: Burney, Woltering, Burke, Naylor, Pasternak 2010, PNAS, “Solar-powered drip irrigation enhances food security in the Sudano-Sahel” (PubMed abstract): Green Revolution technologies had relatively little impact in sub-Saharan Africa, so few such interventions have been rigorously evaluated; matched-pair comparison of villages in northern Benin (two treatment, two comparison); solar-powered drip irrigation significantly augments household income and nutritional intake, particularly in the dry season, and is cost effective compared to alternative technologies; first author's given name Jennifer from the MEDLINE record

items.notes: Technology and engineering (agriculture). Reviewer replacement: the first draft (ultrasound pulses mimicking bat calls to repel pest moths, Nakano et al. 2022) would have been the fifth moth-and-bat subject and the third item on bats or bat calls keeping moths off crops (live corn earworm and rice borer items). Shape of 3.12 and 3.9: problem, evaluation, finding; the key joins both outcomes with the cost point and paraphrases them (earnings, diets, competitive cost). The second sentence's description of drip irrigation is general knowledge; everything else is in the abstract, and the passage keeps its word significantly. Band 6: each wrong option keeps a true part (the setup sentence, the income gain, the diet gain) and fails on one later link.

fixes: replaced the subject (reviewer): the ultrasound moth-repellent study would have been the fifth moth-and-bat subject and the third on bats or bat calls keeping moths off crops (live corn earworm and rice borer items, staged ultrasound bat deterrent); new subject solar-powered drip irrigation in northern Benin (Burney et al. 2010, PubMed abstract fetched), claimed in claims.txt and the old claim withdrawn; new item self-solved A after writing, every option tested against the passage
rephrased one clause that check_rw found shared with live form_structure_and_sense.R1_lex.medium.w2b1_08
review.note: New premise checked against the PubMed abstract and the MEDLINE author record.

band7.why: Replacement item: every wrong option keeps a true part (C the setup sentence, B the income gain, D the diet gain) and fails on one later link (an invented comparison, the setup read as the conclusion, a reversed cost finding); the key paraphrases income, nutrition and cost-effectiveness.

items.passage: Many songbird parents remove their nestlings’ droppings, which are encased in mucous fecal sacs, from the nest, and for roughly forty years this behavior has been explained as a defense against parasites that the sacs would otherwise attract. Though frequently cited as established, that explanation had not been experimentally tested until Juan Diego Ibáñez-Álamo and colleagues positioned fecal sacs near Eurasian blackbird nestlings. The sacs attracted flies but not parasites, and nestlings exposed to them carried no more parasites than others did; what the sacs did increase was an indicator of immune activation in the chicks.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Fecal sacs placed near nests drew flies that carry parasites to the nestlings, which supports the long-standing explanation for why songbirds remove the sacs from their nests.
Ibáñez-Álamo and colleagues found that songbirds remove fecal sacs from their nests mainly to keep flies away from their nestlings.
Because nestlings near fecal sacs showed stronger immune responses, the sacs probably help to protect a brood from parasites.
Experiments did not support a long-accepted reason for songbirds’ removal of fecal sacs, though the sacs did seem to affect the chicks in some other way.
items.explanation: The behavior “has been explained as a defense against parasites,” an explanation “frequently cited as established” but untested. In the experiment, the sacs “attracted flies but not parasites,” and exposed nestlings “carried no more parasites than others did,” yet the sacs did increase “an indicator of immune activation in the chicks.” So the main idea is that the old explanation was not supported, though the sacs seem to affect nestlings in some other way.

A.recipe: contradicts the text (affirms the old view)
A.why_wrong: The sacs attracted flies “but not parasites,” and nestlings near them had no more parasites, so the results do not support the old explanation.

B.why_wrong: The study found that the sacs attract flies, but the text never says that keeping flies away is the main reason the birds remove the sacs.

C.recipe: twisted detail (wrong conclusion from a true result)
C.why_wrong: The text reports the immune response but never links it to protection from parasites; it says that the sacs did not bring more parasites, not that they help guard against them.

sources.what: Ibáñez-Álamo, Ruiz-Raya, Rodríguez, Soler 2016, Frontiers in Zoology: the parasitism hypothesis for fecal sac removal proposed 40 years ago and often cited as demonstrated fact but never tested experimentally; fecal sacs attracted flies but not ectoparasites; fecal sacs near blackbird nestlings did not increase parasites (mites were even reduced); nestlings near feces showed higher H/L ratio, an immune activation; results do not support the parasitism hypothesis

items.notes: Natural science (ornithology). View then correction; the two-part key carries the rejection and the concession. The study's experiments 1 and 2 used traps and artificial nests and experiment 3 active blackbird nests; the passage simplifies to sacs placed near nestlings. Band 6: B and C each keep a true result (flies, immune response) and overreach from it.

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract (parasitism hypothesis untested for 40 years, sacs drew flies not ectoparasites, raised H/L ratio).

band7.why: Two-part key (rejection plus concession); A, B and C each keep a true result (flies drawn, immune activation) and overreach from it, so no wrong option dies on one stated fact alone.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Dora Sigerson Shorter’s 1898 poem “The Scallop Shell.” The speaker and the person the speaker addresses have been watching a scallop shell that the tide has carried away from the shore. A craft is a boat.

It gleamed and passed—you burdened it with love,
With sweet long futures, new and dreamy days:
And named for me—because I held your hopes.
I bid you hush—not meriting your praise.

I pointed, as your vessel came to shore,
Wrecked where the tiny breakers rose and fell;
And bid your voyagers not put to sea
So frail a craft as this poor scallop shell.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The speaker and a companion watch a small shell drift out to sea and grieve together when the waves wreck it near the shore.
The speaker cautions an admirer against entrusting the speaker with hopes that the speaker feels unable to sustain.
The speaker urges a companion to give up dreams of sailing to distant places and to remain on the familiar shore.
The speaker accepts a companion’s praise and promises to carry the companion’s hopes safely through any danger.
items.explanation: The addressee “burdened” the shell with love and hopes and “named” it for the speaker, “because I held your hopes.” The speaker answers, “I bid you hush,” adding that the speaker is “not meriting your praise,” and warns the addressee’s “voyagers” not to set out in “So frail a craft as this poor scallop shell.” The shell stands for the speaker, so the speaker is cautioning the admirer not to place hopes in someone too frail to bear them.

A.why_wrong: The wrecked “vessel” is part of the speaker’s warning about the shell named for the speaker; the poem is not about grieving over a real shell.

C.why_wrong: The “voyagers” are the addressee’s hopes, which the speaker warns against placing in the shell; the poem does not ask anyone to stay home from a real voyage.

D.why_wrong: The speaker tells the addressee to “hush” because the speaker is “not meriting your praise,” so the speaker refuses the praise rather than accepting it.

sources.what: Dora Sigerson Shorter, The Collected Poems of Dora Sigerson Shorter (1907), “The Scallop Shell,” Cornell University Library scan (Harper edition): reads “I pointed, as your vessel came to shore” and “So frail a craft”
Same collection, Hodder and Stoughton 1907 edition (UCLA scan), same wording
First publication: The Fairy Changeling and Other Poems (John Lane, 1898), Project Gutenberg text and Cornell scan; reads “where your vessel” and the misprint “So fail a craft”

items.notes: Poem, extended metaphor (the shell is the speaker, the voyagers are the addressee's hopes). Reviewer changes: text now from the 1907 Collected Poems, whose two scans read “So frail a craft” (the 1898 edition's “fail” was a misprint, so no bracket is needed) and “as your vessel came to shore”; stanza 1 (the shell's description, 34 words) cut at the stanza break, as 3.14 cuts Sonnet 27 at a line boundary, and its literal content carried into the context line, so the verse is 64 words (CB poems 44 to 91, median 67) instead of 98. Gutenberg-style double hyphens set as closed em dashes. Gloss line for craft, as 3.17 glosses its nautical words. Band 6: A and C read the figure literally (A now anchored by the context line), D reverses the speaker's stance.

fixes: re-sourced the text to the 1907 Collected Poems (two scans agree): “So frail a craft” replaces the bracketed [frail] for the 1898 misprint “fail”, and “where your vessel” becomes “as your vessel” as in that edition

verse was 98 words, above CB's 91-word poem maximum and the report's 95-word bound: cut stanza 1 at the stanza break (as 3.14 cuts Sonnet 27) and carried its literal content into the context line; verse now 64 words, near the CB poem median of 67; re-solved B
review.note: Poem checked against the 1898 Gutenberg text, the 1898 Cornell scan and both 1907 Collected Poems scans.

band7.why: Extended metaphor: the key needs the shell mapped to the speaker and the voyagers to the addressee's hopes; A and C are literal readings anchored by the context line and the poem's own nautical words, D reverses the stance.

items.passage: When a flower changes color over its lifetime, the transformation almost invariably proceeds in one direction, and it may signal to pollinators which blossoms still offer a reward. Hirokazu Tsukaya and colleagues documented a remarkable exception in Causonis japonica, a climbing vine in the grape family. Each flower’s central disc is orange during the flower’s initial male phase and fades to pink once the stamens detach; several hours later, as the female structures mature, the disc returns to orange before fading to pink again. Nectar secretion roughly corresponded to these shifts.
items.stem: According to the text, what is unusual about the color changes in the flowers of Causonis japonica?
options: They are caused by pigments that differ from those responsible for color changes in other flowers.
They show pollinators which flowers hold the most nectar, unlike the color changes of other flowers.
They reverse and then repeat, whereas the color changes of nearly all other flowers move in a single direction.
They take place only during the female phase, after the stamens have detached.
items.explanation: The text says that color change in flowers “almost invariably proceeds in one direction,” but in Causonis japonica the disc goes from orange to pink, “returns to orange,” and then fades “to pink again.” What is unusual is that the change reverses and repeats.

A.why_wrong: The text never says which pigments cause the changes or compares them with the pigments of other flowers.

B.why_wrong: The text says that color changes in general can signal rewards to pollinators, so this is not what sets Causonis japonica apart; nectar secretion only “roughly corresponded” to its shifts.

D.why_wrong: The disc is orange and then pink during the male phase as well, so the changes are not limited to the female phase.

sources.what: Furukawa, Tsukaya, Kawakubo 2022, Scientific Reports: all previously reported flower colour changes are unidirectional (one incomplete exception); in Causonis japonica (Vitaceae) flower discs are orange in the male phase, fade to pink as stamens drop, recover orange with stigma maturation hours later, then fade to pink again; nectar secretion roughly correlated; colour change may be an honest signal to pollinators

items.notes: Natural science (botany). Explicit detail; the stem's word unusual points to the contrast with the first sentence. Carotenoids left out of the passage (A is therefore unsupported, not contradicted). Hirokazu Tsukaya (University of Tokyo) is the corresponding author, given name confirmed from his other PubMed records; the first author's given name was not available, so he is not named.

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract; the passage names Hirokazu Tsukaya, the corresponding author (first author Furukawa), which is a real author of the study.

items.passage: During the Second World War, the Comet Line, an escape network organized by Belgian resistance member Andrée de Jongh, guided Allied airmen who had been shot down over occupied Belgium and France across the Pyrenees into Spain; de Jongh herself made two dozen round trips over the mountains. The network accepted financial assistance from British intelligence but, until 1943, declined its repeated offers of radios and radio operators. Its leaders had observed that resistance groups were frequently dismantled after the Germans captured a radio, so the network relied instead on couriers to transport messages to British diplomats in Spain.
items.stem: According to the text, why did the Comet Line decline the radios offered by British intelligence?
options: Its leaders had seen other resistance groups collapse after the Germans seized a radio.
Its leaders did not want British intelligence to learn the routes that its couriers followed.
Its members could not carry heavy radio equipment safely over the Pyrenees.
Its couriers could already reach British diplomats in Spain faster than radio messages could.
items.explanation: The text explains that the network’s leaders “had observed that resistance groups were frequently dismantled after the Germans captured a radio,” and that this is why the network “relied instead on couriers.” So the leaders turned down radios because captured radios had led to the downfall of other groups.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about keeping the couriers’ routes secret from British intelligence, which the line accepted money from and sent messages to.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions the trips across the Pyrenees, but it never says that radio equipment was too heavy to carry there.

D.why_wrong: The text says that couriers carried messages to diplomats in Spain, but it never compares the speed of couriers with that of radio messages.

sources.what: Comet Line, Wikipedia: Belgian escape line organized by Andrée de Jongh; airmen escorted through France across the Pyrenees to Spain; de Jongh made 24 round trips; financial assistance from MI9; until 1943 the line denied British offers of radios and radio operators because resistance groups were often broken up by the Germans after a radio was captured; couriers carried messages to and from British diplomats in Spain

items.notes: History. Explicit detail answered by one sentence; B to D are reasons a student might supply from the setting (secrecy, the mountains, speed).

review.note: Wikipedia Comet Line confirms MI9 money, radios and operators declined until 1943 because captured radios broke up groups, couriers to diplomats in Spain, 24 round trips.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Mazo de la Roche’s 1922 novel Explorers of the Dawn. The narrator is describing a parlour in the house where he and his brothers live. Mary Ellen is a servant there.

On other week days the shutters of this grim apartment were kept closed, and an inquisitive eye, applied to the keyhole, could just faintly discern the portrait in crayon of the late Mr. Handsomebody, presiding, like some whiskered ghost, over the revels of the stuffed birds in the glass case below him.

But on a Saturday morning Mary Ellen swept and dusted there. Moreover Mary Ellen liked our company. She had a spooky feeling about the parlour. Mr. Handsomebody gave her the creeps, she said, and once when she had turned her back she had heard one of the stuffed birds twitter.
items.stem: According to the text, why does Mary Ellen like having company in the parlour?
options: They help her with the sweeping and dusting so that she can finish quickly.
She enjoys showing them the portrait of the late Mr. Handsomebody.
She believes that the stuffed birds are less likely to be damaged when they are there.
She feels uneasy in the room and is glad to have others there with her.
items.explanation: Right after saying that “Mary Ellen liked our company,” the narrator explains that “She had a spooky feeling about the parlour”: the portrait of “Mr. Handsomebody gave her the creeps,” and she once thought she “heard one of the stuffed birds twitter.” She likes the boys’ company because the room makes her uneasy.

A.why_wrong: The text says that Mary Ellen swept and dusted the parlour, but it never says that the boys helped her or that she was racing to finish.

B.why_wrong: The portrait of Mr. Handsomebody “gave her the creeps,” so she would not enjoy showing it off.

C.why_wrong: The stuffed birds frighten Mary Ellen (she thought she heard one “twitter”); nothing suggests that she worries about their being damaged.

sources.what: Mazo de la Roche, Explorers of the Dawn (Knopf, 1922), chapter I, “Buried Treasure,” Project Gutenberg text

items.notes: Literary prose. Excerpt copied exactly; one sentence (the shutters thrown open and the furniture furbished) trimmed from the second paragraph to keep the length near the model's; the preceding sentence about the boys' guardian, Mrs. Handsomebody, going to market each Saturday and the closing sentence (“It was a gruesome thought.”) left out. Gutenberg quotes made curly. British spelling parlour kept from the text and stem.

fixes: attribution changed to “adapted from”: the excerpt drops a sentence inside the second paragraph
review.note: Excerpt checked word for word against Gutenberg 25283 (one sentence trimmed inside the second paragraph).

items.passage: Studies of how cephalopods camouflage themselves against the seafloor have concentrated on cuttlefish and octopuses, which typically rest on the bottom. Oval squid, by contrast, are semi-pelagic, inhabiting mostly the open water above it. Nevertheless, when Ryuta Nakajima and colleagues kept oval squid from Okinawa, Japan, in tanks, the animals adjusted the pigment cells in their skin to correspond to the substrate beneath them, modifying their patterning whenever they moved over a bottom of different reflectivity, a capacity never previously documented in the laboratory for any squid in their family.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Research has shown that oval squid match their skin to the seafloor more rapidly than cuttlefish and octopuses do.
Research indicates that oval squid, though they rarely rest on the seafloor, can change their coloring to match it.
Researchers have found that oval squid in Okinawa change their skin patterns mainly to communicate in open water.
Because oval squid spend little time near the seafloor, they lack the pigment cells needed to match it.
items.explanation: The text contrasts cuttlefish and octopuses, which “typically rest on the bottom,” with oval squid, which inhabit “mostly the open water above it.” Even so, in tanks the squid “adjusted the pigment cells in their skin to correspond to the substrate beneath them.” The main idea is that oval squid, despite their open-water habits, can match the seafloor.

A.why_wrong: The text never compares how quickly oval squid, cuttlefish, and octopuses change color.

C.why_wrong: The squid changed their patterning in response to the bottom beneath them; the text says nothing about using color to communicate.

D.why_wrong: The squid “adjusted the pigment cells in their skin,” so they do have pigment cells that let them match the seafloor.

sources.what: Nakajima, Lajbner, Kuba et al. 2022, Scientific Reports: camouflage-to-substrate studies have focused on benthic cuttlefish and octopus; oval squid (Sepioteuthis lessoniana species complex) are semi-pelagic; in captivity S. lessoniana Sp. 2 from Okinawa adapts chromatophore coloration to the background substrate and changes patterning when moving between substrates of different reflectivity; not reported before in any loliginid under laboratory conditions

items.notes: Natural science (marine biology). Study report with a contrast (benthic vs semi-pelagic); key generalizes the finding. Ryuta Nakajima is the first author. Overlap check: no live item on cephalopod background matching (the squid items are vampire, bobtail, firefly and giant squid).

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract (semi-pelagic oval squid from Okinawa match substrate in captivity; not reported before for any loliginid in the lab).

items.passage: The sculptor known as the Master of Rimini carved large numbers of alabaster figures around 1420 to 1440, and art historians have generally placed his workshop in Flanders or northern France, chiefly because his sculptures resemble Flemish and French paintings. When Wolfram Kloppmann and colleagues measured isotopes in the stone of works attributed to the master and his workshop, however, they found that all were carved from alabaster quarried in Franconia, in present-day northern Bavaria, some 600 kilometers away. The researchers therefore propose that the workshop operated in southern Germany.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers have shown that the Master of Rimini learned to carve alabaster from sculptors who were working in Franconia.
The resemblance between the Master of Rimini’s sculptures and Flemish paintings shows that he was trained in the Low Countries.
Analysis of the stone in the Master of Rimini’s sculptures has led researchers to place his workshop in Germany, not Flanders or France.
Because alabaster was traded widely across medieval Europe, the source of a sculpture’s stone reveals little about where the sculpture was actually carved.
items.explanation: Art historians placed the workshop “in Flanders or northern France” because of the sculptures’ style, but Kloppmann and colleagues found that all the works were “carved from alabaster quarried in Franconia,” far from that region, and so “propose that the workshop operated in southern Germany.” The main idea is that the stone has led researchers to place the workshop in Germany instead.

A.why_wrong: The text says that the alabaster came from Franconia, not that the master learned his craft from sculptors there.

B.recipe: overstated (old evidence pushed to a conclusion)
B.why_wrong: The text says only that the resemblance led historians to place the workshop in Flanders or France; it never says that he trained in the Low Countries.

D.why_wrong: The researchers used the source of the stone to propose where the workshop was, so they treat it as revealing a great deal.

sources.what: Kloppmann et al. 2022, PLoS ONE: isotope fingerprints (Sr, S, O) of works attributed to the Master of Rimini (active about 1420 to 1440) and his workshop are virtually identical; material exclusively Franconian (northern Bavarian) alabaster, 600 km from the supposed Flemish or northern French workshop, whose location rested on similarities with Flemish and French painting; researchers propose a workshop in southern Germany

items.notes: Arts and humanities (art history). The key carries both halves (old placement and the revision), at medium length. The paper also suggests that the master may have trained in the Low Countries; the passage leaves this out, so B overreaches from the stylistic evidence the passage gives.

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract (Franconian alabaster 600 km away; prevailing Flemish or N-French attribution rests on painting parallels; southern German workshop proposed).

items.passage: The Libri Picturati, a collection of plant illustrations produced in the seventeenth-century Dutch colony in Brazil and now preserved in a library in Kraków, Poland, has primarily been studied for its artistic qualities. Mireia Alcàntara-Rodríguez and colleagues instead identified the plants depicted, which comprise 198 taxa, predominantly wild trees native to the rainforest. The illustrations also contain the earliest known record in Brazil of the Ethiopian pepper, a tree native to Africa.
items.stem: Based on the text, what can be concluded about the Ethiopian pepper?
options: It was present in Brazil by the 1600s despite originating elsewhere.
It was among the most widespread plants growing in the Dutch colony in Brazil at the time.
It was painted more often than any of the native rainforest trees in the collection.
It was first described as a distinct species by Alcàntara-Rodríguez and colleagues.
items.explanation: The text says that the illustrations were “produced in the seventeenth-century Dutch colony in Brazil” and that they contain “the earliest known record in Brazil of the Ethiopian pepper, a tree native to Africa.” So the plant had reached Brazil by the 1600s, though it came from elsewhere.

B.why_wrong: The text says that the Ethiopian pepper appears in the illustrations, not that it was common in the colony.

C.why_wrong: The 198 taxa are “predominantly wild trees native to the rainforest”; nothing says that the Ethiopian pepper was painted more often than any of them.

D.why_wrong: Alcàntara-Rodríguez and colleagues identified the plants in the illustrations; the text never says that they were the first to describe any species.

sources.what: Alcàntara-Rodríguez, Françozo, van Andel 2021, Scientific Reports: the Libri Picturati, plant illustrations from seventeenth-century Dutch Brazil kept in the Jagiellonian library in Kraków since World War II; earlier studies focused on artistic details and history; 198 taxa identified, mostly wild native rainforest trees, 35 introduced species; first records of the Ethiopian pepper in Brazil
Ethiopian pepper (Xylopia aethiopica) is native to tropical Africa

items.notes: Arts and humanities with natural science (history of botany). One-step inference, as in 2.19: painted in the colony in the 1600s plus native to Africa, so present in Brazil by then though not native. The paper also names the sunflower; left out (another item in this batch is about sunflower pollen). Author names confirmed from the PubMed record; the Ethiopian pepper's native range from the fetched Wikipedia page (an evergreen tree native to Africa).

review.note: Abstract confirms the 198 taxa, mostly native rainforest trees, and the first record of the Ethiopian pepper in Brazil; Wikipedia Xylopia aethiopica confirms it is native to Africa.

items.passage: In the 1960s, British artist Tom Phillips came across a forgotten Victorian novel, William Hurrell Mallock’s A Human Document, and began painting, drawing, and collaging over its pages, leaving only scattered fragments of the original text visible. Read in sequence, those surviving words constitute an entirely new narrative about a character named Bill Toge, whose name can appear only where Mallock happened to write “together” or “altogether.” Phillips published the result as A Humument in 1970 and continued replacing pages in subsequent editions until 2016.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Phillips set out to rescue a forgotten Victorian novel by drawing new readers to Mallock’s original story.
Phillips’s A Humument is admired mainly for the images that cover its pages rather than for its story.
Over the decades, Phillips’s pages have grown steadily less abstract as he has allowed more of Mallock’s original words to show through.
Phillips created a new story by covering most of an existing novel’s text and keeping only some of its words.
items.explanation: Phillips painted and collaged over the pages of “a forgotten Victorian novel,” “leaving only scattered fragments of the original text visible,” and those words “constitute an entirely new narrative about a character named Bill Toge.” The main idea is that he made a new work and a new story out of an existing book.

A.recipe: twisted detail (example turned into a purpose)
A.why_wrong: Phillips covered most of Mallock’s words to tell a new story; the text never says that he wanted readers to read Mallock’s novel.

B.why_wrong: The text never says how A Humument is received or which part of it is most admired.

C.recipe: chronological story the text does not tell
C.why_wrong: The text says that Phillips continued replacing pages, but it never says that the pages became less abstract or showed more of Mallock’s words.

sources.what: A Humument, Wikipedia: altered book by Tom Phillips over W. H. Mallock’s 1892 novel A Human Document, begun in the 1960s, first edition 1970, completed 2016; Phillips drew, painted and collaged over the pages leaving some original text visible; new story with protagonist Bill Toge, whose name appears only where together or altogether appears; later editions revise and replace pages

items.notes: Arts and humanities (visual art, artist's book). Profile: aim and method, one concrete detail (Bill Toge), effect. Key generalizes the method; distractors follow the T3 recipes (example as purpose, invented reputation, invented chronology).

review.note: Wikipedia A Humument confirms the method, Bill Toge from together or altogether, 1970 first edition and 2016 completion.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Winifred Holtby’s 1924 novel The Crowded Street. Eleven-year-old Muriel has come to a children’s dance with her mother, Mrs. Hammond.

“It’s nearly time to begin dancing,” said Muriel’s mother. “We must get your programme filled. There are a lot of little boys here whom you know. Look, there’s Freddy Mason. You remember him, dear, don’t you?”

“I don’t think—” she began in her prim little voice. She was about to add—“that I want to dance with Freddy,” when Mrs. Hammond finished her sentence for her.

“Of course he’ll want to dance with you, dear.” Mrs. Hammond claimed that she knew what went on in Muriel’s mind—her own child’s mind. She often finished Muriel’s hesitating sentences for her. “You mustn’t be so shy, dear,” she reproved gently.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Muriel is too shy to speak to Freddy, so her mother kindly steps in and introduces the two children to each other.
Muriel and her mother argue about whether Freddy would be a suitable partner until Muriel gives in.
Muriel’s mother, sure that she knows her daughter’s thoughts, answers for Muriel and overlooks the girl’s actual wishes.
Mrs. Hammond gently scolds Muriel for having been rude to Freddy the last time they met.
items.explanation: Muriel starts to say that she does not want to dance with Freddy, but Mrs. Hammond “finished her sentence for her” with the opposite meaning. The text explains that Mrs. Hammond “claimed that she knew what went on in Muriel’s mind” and “often finished Muriel’s hesitating sentences.” So the main idea is that the mother, sure she knows Muriel’s thoughts, speaks for her and misses her real wish.

A.why_wrong: Mrs. Hammond calls Muriel shy, but Muriel is trying to say that she does not want to dance with Freddy; the mother overrides her rather than helping her.

B.why_wrong: There is no argument: Muriel never finishes her sentence, and her mother does not realize that Muriel objects.

D.why_wrong: Mrs. Hammond “reproved gently” for shyness, not for rudeness, and the text never mentions Muriel being rude to Freddy.

sources.what: Winifred Holtby, The Crowded Street (1924), prologue, Project Gutenberg text

items.notes: Literary prose. Excerpt copied exactly with one paragraph trimmed between the first and second paragraphs (Muriel's memory of a frightening fall from a haystack while playing with Freddy, ending “But she did not now want to dance with Freddy”); Gutenberg's double and quadruple hyphens set as closed em dashes and quotes made curly. Key: speaker's state and situation in plain terms, as in the T4 models.

fixes: attribution changed to “adapted from”: the excerpt drops a whole paragraph between kept paragraphs
review.note: Excerpt checked word for word against Gutenberg 68629 (one paragraph trimmed); Muriel is eleven in the prologue.

items.passage: The cemetery of Jebel Sahaba, in the Nile Valley of northern Sudan, holds the remains of 61 people buried at least 13,400 years ago, many of them bearing injuries inflicted by weapons. Since the site was excavated in the 1960s, it has often been interpreted as the record of a single conflict. However, when Isabelle Crevecoeur and colleagues reexamined the skeletons microscopically, they identified more than 100 previously undocumented injuries, and a quarter of the individuals with injuries had both healed and unhealed wounds.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers have confirmed that most of the people buried at Jebel Sahaba died in a single conflict, as the original excavators had proposed.
A reexamination of the Jebel Sahaba skeletons suggests that the people buried there faced repeated violence, not a single conflict.
Crevecoeur and colleagues found that the injuries at Jebel Sahaba were caused by different weapons than earlier researchers had believed.
Because many of the injuries at Jebel Sahaba had healed, researchers now doubt that the site records any violence at all.
items.explanation: The site “has often been interpreted as the record of a single conflict,” but the reexamination found that “a quarter of the individuals with injuries had both healed and unhealed wounds.” People who survived earlier injuries and then received new ones were caught up in violence more than once, so the main idea is that the violence recurred rather than occurring in a single conflict.

A.recipe: contradicts the text (affirms the earlier view)
A.why_wrong: The healed and unhealed wounds point away from a single conflict, and the text presents the reexamination as challenging that view.

C.why_wrong: The text says that the injuries were “inflicted by weapons” but never discusses which weapons or compares the findings with earlier beliefs about them.

D.why_wrong: The reexamination found even more injuries than before, so it adds evidence of violence rather than casting doubt on it.

sources.what: Crevecoeur, Dias-Meirinho, Zazzo, Antoine, Bon 2021, Scientific Reports: Jebel Sahaba cemetery (site 117), 61 individuals, at least 13.4 ka; excavated in the 1960s; over 100 previously undocumented healed and unhealed lesions; most from projectile weapons; a quarter of skeletons with lesions show both healed and unhealed trauma; the hypothesis of a single warfare event is dismissed in favor of sporadic, recurrent episodes of interpersonal violence

items.notes: Archaeology. View then correction; the passage gives the evidence (healed plus unhealed wounds) and leaves the conclusion (recurrent violence) for the key. Kept clinical: no description of wounds beyond healed and unhealed.

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract (over 100 new lesions, a quarter with healed and unhealed trauma, single warfare event dismissed).

items.passage: Many restaurants in Japan display their dishes, from bowls of ramen to plates of sushi, in the front window as replicas known as shokuhin sampuru. The models are mostly handcrafted from polyvinyl chloride, and a restaurant ordering a complete menu of them may pay more than a million yen. Why would restaurants spend so much on food that no one can eat? Unlike real dishes, the replicas can remain on display indefinitely without spoiling or attracting insects. Moreover, when artisans began producing such models in the late 1920s, written menus were uncommon in Japan, so the replicas allowed customers to order simply by looking.
items.stem: Which question does the text most directly attempt to answer?
options: Why do many restaurants in Japan pay for expensive replicas of the dishes they serve?
How do artisans make shokuhin sampuru look so much like real food?
Which dishes are most often reproduced as shokuhin sampuru?
Why have some restaurants in Japan stopped displaying shokuhin sampuru?
items.explanation: After describing the replicas and their cost, the text asks, “Why would restaurants spend so much on food that no one can eat?” It then answers: the replicas can stay on display “without spoiling or attracting insects,” and they “allowed customers to order simply by looking.” So the text mainly addresses why restaurants pay for such replicas.

B.recipe: on-topic question the text never takes up
B.why_wrong: The text says that the models are handcrafted from polyvinyl chloride, but it does not explain how they are made to look real.

C.recipe: on-topic question the text never takes up
C.why_wrong: Ramen and sushi are given as examples, but the text never says which dishes are reproduced most often.

D.recipe: on-topic question the text never takes up
D.why_wrong: The text never mentions restaurants that have stopped using the replicas.

sources.what: Food model (shokuhin sampuru), Wikipedia: models mostly handmade from polyvinyl chloride; a complete menu can cost a restaurant over a million yen; replicas avoid displaying real food that may spoil or attract insects and can last indefinitely; in the late 1920s artisans developed models that made it easy to order without menus, which were not common in Japan then

items.notes: Social science (culture and business). Central-question template: the passage poses its own question and answers it; the key restates that question. Distractor questions are on-topic but unanswered, and differ from 2.20's (no first-use, how-many or other-countries frames).

fixes: source URL changed to the redirect target (Food model)
review.note: Wikipedia Food model confirms PVC, over a million yen for a full menu, no spoiling or insects, late-1920s origin when menus were uncommon.

items.passage: Canadian folk artist Maud Lewis lived for decades in a one-room house in Marshalltown, Nova Scotia. She initially sold hand-painted Christmas cards and eventually sold brightly colored paintings of oxen, horses, cats, and boats directly from her home. Lewis painted the same subjects repeatedly, each time slightly differently, partly because her customers kept requesting them. She also decorated almost every surface of her tiny house, including the walls, doors, and stove, with painted flowers and leaves. Although Lewis lived in poverty, her cheerful pictures eventually earned her national recognition in the mid-1960s.
items.stem: According to the text, what is one reason Lewis painted the same subjects many times?
options: She had first painted those subjects on the Christmas cards that she sold.
She seldom left her small house to look for new subjects to paint.
People who bought her work kept asking for those subjects.
She wanted her paintings to match the flowers she had painted on her walls.
items.explanation: The text says that Lewis painted the same subjects “repeatedly, each time slightly differently, partly because her customers kept requesting them.” So one reason is that buyers kept asking for those subjects.

A.why_wrong: The text says that Lewis initially sold Christmas cards, but it never says that the cards showed the subjects she later repeated.

B.why_wrong: The text says that Lewis lived in a one-room house, but it never says that she rarely left it or that this limited her subjects.

D.why_wrong: Lewis painted flowers and leaves on her walls, but the text never links her repeated subjects to those decorations.

sources.what: Maud Lewis, Wikipedia: Nova Scotia folk artist; lived in poverty in a one-room house in Marshalltown; national recognition in 1964 and 1965; began selling hand-painted Christmas cards, later sold cards and paintings from her home; subjects included oxen, horses, cats and Cape Island boats; returned to the same subjects again and again, each time slightly differently, partly motivated by customer demand; painted walls, doors, breadboxes and the stove

items.notes: Arts (folk painting). Explicit detail; stem frame “what is one reason,” as in 1.2 and 1.9. Each distractor reuses a real detail of the passage (cards, the small house, the painted walls) in a link the text never makes.

review.note: Wikipedia Maud Lewis confirms repeated subjects partly motivated by customer demand, Christmas cards, painted house and stove, recognition in 1964 and 1965.

items.passage: In 1911, Cora Wilson Stewart, the superintendent of schools in Rowan County, Kentucky, established what she called Moonlight Schools, where adults who could not read attended evening classes in the same schoolhouses that children used during the day. Volunteer teachers traveled from house to house to recruit students. Because no reading textbooks had been written for adults who were just learning to read, Stewart published a newspaper for them that used only a limited vocabulary.
items.stem: According to the text, why did Stewart publish a newspaper for students in the Moonlight Schools?
options: She wanted to let adults in Rowan County know when the classes would meet.
The students had asked her for news about their own communities.
The volunteer teachers needed a way to find adults who could not read.
No reading books existed that were suited to adults who were beginning to read.
items.explanation: The text says that Stewart published the newspaper because “no reading textbooks had been written for adults who were just learning to read.” The newspaper filled that gap.

A.why_wrong: The text never says that the newspaper announced when classes met.

B.why_wrong: The text never says that the students asked for local news.

C.why_wrong: The volunteer teachers recruited students by traveling “from house to house”; the newspaper was for the students, not a way to find them.

sources.what: Moonlight School, Wikipedia: first Moonlight School created in September 1911 in Rowan County, Kentucky, by superintendent Cora Wilson Stewart; adults attended at night in buildings where children studied by day; volunteer teachers canvassed their districts; there were no school books for adults who could not read, so a newspaper was published with a very small word list

items.notes: History (education). Explicit detail stated with because in one sentence; C reuses the canvassing detail. The detail that the schools are said to have met on moonlit nights is left out.

review.note: Wikipedia Moonlight School confirms 1911, Rowan County, Stewart as superintendent, night classes in day schoolhouses, canvassing volunteers, the small-vocabulary newspaper because no adult readers existed.

items.passage:
The following text is from Margaret Wilson’s 1923 novel The Able McLaughlins. Davie and Sarah, who are not yet old enough to attend school, have been watching a frisky calf with their older brother Hughie on the family’s prairie farm.

Hughie was not, like the others, at home because he was too small to go to school. Indeed, no! Hughie was ten, and at home to-day because he had been chilling, the day before, with the fever that rose from the newly-broken prairie. The three of them sat quiet only a moment.

“Why does he frisk his tail so?” Davie asked.

“He’s praising the Lord,” replied Hughie, wise and wan.
items.stem: According to the text, why is Hughie at home instead of at school?
options: He is too young to go to school.
He was ill with a fever on the previous day.
He was asked by his parents to look after the calf.
He is keeping watch over Davie and Sarah.
items.explanation: The text says that Hughie was “at home to-day because he had been chilling, the day before, with the fever that rose from the newly-broken prairie.” He stayed home because he had been sick the day before.

A.recipe: contradicts the text (the reason the text rules out)
A.why_wrong: The text says that Hughie was not at home “because he was too small to go to school”; that is why Davie and Sarah are at home, but Hughie is ten.

C.why_wrong: Hughie is watching the calf with the younger children, but the text never says that he was asked to look after it.

D.why_wrong: Hughie is with Davie and Sarah, but the text gives his illness, not caring for them, as the reason he is home.

sources.what: Margaret Wilson, The Able McLaughlins (1923), chapter I, Project Gutenberg text

items.notes: Literary prose. Excerpt copied exactly (one paragraph and two lines of dialogue, consecutive in the novel); the preceding paragraphs about the calf are summed up in the context line. Like 1.19, the obvious detail (too small for school) is the trap, here one the text explicitly denies for Hughie.

review.note: Excerpt checked word for word against Gutenberg 59845.

items.passage: Every spring in Austria, common frogs leave the places where they spent the winter and travel to ponds to breed, and many are killed on roads along the way. Temporary protective measures can save them, but only if those measures are in place in time. Analyzing thousands of observations recorded by volunteers, Maria Peer and colleagues found that the frogs’ migration closely followed the flowering of certain plants, such as goat willow and apricot trees. The researchers suggest that such flowering could signal when protections should be set up.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that the flowering of certain plants could help people predict when common frogs will begin migrating.
Volunteers in Austria have built barriers that keep most common frogs from being killed on roads.
Common frogs decide when to migrate by watching for the blossoms of goat willow and apricot trees.
Researchers have shown that roads are the main cause of the decline of frogs in Austria.
items.explanation: Peer and colleagues “found that the frogs’ migration closely followed the flowering of certain plants,” and they “suggest that such flowering could signal when protections should be set up.” The main idea is that plant flowering could help predict when the frogs will migrate.

B.why_wrong: The text says that volunteers recorded observations and that temporary measures can save frogs, but it never says that volunteers built barriers that protect most frogs.

C.why_wrong: The migration “closely followed” the flowering; the text never says that the frogs watch for blossoms.

D.why_wrong: The text says that many frogs are killed on roads, not that roads are the main cause of a decline.

sources.what: Peer, Dörler, Zaller et al. 2021, Scientific Reports: roads disrupt amphibian migration between hibernation and breeding sites, causing roadkill; timely temporary mitigation measures needed; 3,751 amphibian and 7,818 plant phenology observations from Austrian citizen science; common frog migration closely associated with phenology of European larch, goat willow and apricot; plant phenology can be used to time temporary mitigation measures

items.notes: Natural science (ecology). Easy study report, main idea in the last sentence as in 1.8 and 1.10, key hedged with could to match suggest. The study also covered common toads (weaker association), left out.

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract (Austrian citizen-science data; common frog migration closely tied to goat willow and apricot phenology; timing of temporary measures).

items.passage: Psychologist David Brieber and colleagues investigated whether the setting in which people encounter art affects how they respond to it. Two groups of participants viewed the artworks from an exhibition, one group in a museum and the other in a laboratory, while a mobile eye-tracking device recorded how long each person examined each work. Afterward, participants evaluated the works. Participants in the museum looked at the artworks longer, considered them more interesting, and liked them more than participants in the laboratory did.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that wearing eye-tracking devices causes people to spend less time looking at art.
Psychologists found that people prefer paintings to other kinds of art, whether in a museum or a laboratory.
A study showed that people enjoy art more when they view it with a group of friends than when they view it by themselves.
A study found that people respond more favorably to artworks when they see them in a museum than in a laboratory.
items.explanation: The researchers compared viewers “in a museum” with viewers “in a laboratory,” and participants in the museum “looked at the artworks longer, considered them more interesting, and liked them more.” So the main idea is that people respond more favorably to art seen in a museum.

A.why_wrong: Both groups wore the eye-tracking device, so the study could not show that the device itself shortened viewing time.

B.why_wrong: The text never compares paintings with other kinds of art.

C.why_wrong: The two groups saw the art in different places; the text never compares viewing in a group with viewing alone.

sources.what: Brieber, Nadal, Leder, Rosenberg 2014, PLoS ONE: two groups viewed an art exhibition, one in the museum and one in the laboratory, with viewing time recorded by a mobile eye tracking system; participants then rated the artworks; museum participants liked the artworks more, found them more interesting, and viewed them longer

items.notes: Social science (psychology of art). Easy study report like 1.11. Overlap note: a live Words in Context item uses the Met's average viewing time per artwork (Smith and Smith 2001); this item's premise is the museum versus laboratory comparison.

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract. Overlap judged: the live WiC item words_in_context.B5.medium.w2b1_07 is about how briefly Met visitors look at masterpieces; this premise is the museum-versus-laboratory context effect on liking, so it is a different claim, not a clone; kept.

items.passage:
The following text is from E. M. Delafield’s 1919 novel Consequences. Alex, the eldest of several children, has been explaining a new game to her siblings. Emily, the nursery-maid who is supervising them, has just praised her.

“Quite right, Miss Alex; what a clever girl, to be sure. Here, Master Baby, you can play with me. You’re too little to do it all by yourself.”

“He isn’t Baby any more. We’ve got to call him Archie now. The new little sister is Baby,” said Alex dictatorially.

She liked always to be the one to give information, and Emily had only been with them a little while.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Alex is embarrassed that Emily has praised her in front of the other children.
Alex is jealous that her little brother is getting so much of Emily’s attention.
Alex enjoys being the one who tells others how things are, even when the other person is an adult.
Alex is unsure what the family has decided to call the new baby.
items.explanation: When Emily calls the little boy “Master Baby,” Alex corrects her “dictatorially,” explaining that he is now Archie and that “The new little sister is Baby.” The narrator adds that Alex “liked always to be the one to give information.” So the main idea is that Alex enjoys telling others how things are, even an adult such as Emily.

A.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that Alex is embarrassed; she answers Emily’s praise by correcting her with confidence.

B.why_wrong: Alex speaks up when Emily addresses her brother, but the text explains her remark by her liking “to be the one to give information,” not by jealousy.

D.why_wrong: Alex states plainly, “The new little sister is Baby,” so she is not unsure.

sources.what: E. M. Delafield, Consequences (1919), chapter I, “The Game of Consequences,” Project Gutenberg text

items.notes: Literary prose. Three consecutive paragraphs copied exactly (Gutenberg's straight quotes made curly); the opening paragraphs, in which Alex explains the game, are summed up in the context line. Easy: the narrator states the trait outright, and the key restates it in plain terms.

review.note: Excerpt checked word for word against Gutenberg 34935.

items.passage: The Human Library, which began in Copenhagen, Denmark, in 2000, operates much like a conventional library, except that its “books” are people. Each “book” is someone who has experienced prejudice or exclusion, and visitors can “borrow” one for a conversation, asking questions they might never otherwise have the chance to ask. The organization’s goal is to help participants examine their own assumptions about others. The first event, held at Denmark’s Roskilde Festival, drew more than 1,000 participants, and the organization is now active in more than 85 countries.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The Human Library lends out books in which people who have faced prejudice describe their own lives in their own words.
The Human Library aims to challenge prejudice through conversations with people who have experienced it.
The Human Library started as a festival event and has since replaced traditional libraries in many countries.
The Human Library trains librarians to recommend books about prejudice to their visitors.
items.explanation: In the Human Library, the “books” are people who have “experienced prejudice or exclusion,” and visitors “borrow” them for conversations. The organization’s goal is “to help participants examine their own assumptions about others.” So the main idea is that the organization uses conversations to challenge prejudice.

A.recipe: twisted detail (the library analogy taken literally)
A.why_wrong: The text puts “books” in quotation marks because the books are people; visitors talk with them rather than reading written life stories.

C.why_wrong: The text says that the first event was held at a festival and that the organization is active in many countries, not that it has replaced traditional libraries.

D.why_wrong: The text never mentions librarians or recommending books.

sources.what: The Human Library, Wikipedia: began in Copenhagen in 2000 with the first event at the Roskilde Festival (more than 1,000 participants); aims to address prejudice by helping people talk to those they would not normally meet; lends people rather than books, people who have experienced prejudice, social exclusion or stigma; readers ask questions to challenge their own prejudices; active in over 85 countries

items.notes: Social science (civic organization). Profile: aim, method, example, reach; the key generalizes the method and aim. A takes the library analogy literally, C and D are the invented-reach and invented-method recipes.
